blocks.text: 1. Retrieval Planning

blocks.alt: A complex query builds a retrieval plan producing multiple searches

blocks.text: Dynamic Routing showed queries being routed between different retrieval strategies. Retrieval Planning, deciding the retrieval strategy for a query before executing any search, goes one level deeper, planning the retrieval steps within a single query rather than just picking one strategy for the whole thing.
It analyzes the query first to choose how many searches, in what order, and using which strategy.
2. Planning Applied Specifically To Retrieval
General agentic planning sequences tool calls of any kind toward a goal, the same decomposition idea covered generally in Planning.
Retrieval planning is that same idea narrowed specifically to retrieval calls.

blocks.text: 3. Deciding How Many Searches Are Needed

blocks.alt: A query produces an estimated search count

blocks.text: Retrieval planning estimates the number of searches a query will actually require, the same idea as identifying how many hops are needed in Multi-Hop RAG.
It does this before running a single one of them.
4. Choosing A Search Strategy Per Query Part

blocks.alt: Query part A uses semantic search while query part B uses keyword search

blocks.text: Different parts of a complex query can call for different retrieval strategies, the same kind of judgment call as recognizing when Self-RAG is worth its training requirement.
One part might need keyword search while another needs semantic search.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A query asking for both an exact product code and a general comparison benefits from keyword search for the code and semantic search for the comparison, two different strategies within one retrieval plan.

blocks.text: 5. Ordering Searches By Dependency

blocks.alt: Search A leads to search B, which depends on A

blocks.text: A later search often needs a fact from an earlier search as its input, the same reason ordering matters when steps depend on each other in Planning.
The retrieval plan's search order is not arbitrary either.

blocks.text: 6. Retrieval Planning Versus Dynamic Routing

blocks.alt: Retrieval planning builds a multi-step strategy while dynamic routing makes a single decision

blocks.text: Dynamic routing picks one path for a whole query, while retrieval planning can mix several strategies within a single query, extending the routing between retrieval strategies idea from Dynamic Routing.
It is a finer grained decision than routing the whole query at once.
7. Revising The Plan When A Search Comes Up Empty

blocks.alt: An empty search result leads to a revised plan

blocks.text: A search that returns nothing useful can invalidate the rest of the original retrieval plan, the same reason plans need to adapt to new information in Planning.
The plan needs to adjust rather than blindly continuing to the next planned search.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A planned second search that assumed the first search would return a specific entity name must be revised if that first search actually returns nothing, echoing the same plan adaptation covered generally in Planning.

blocks.text: 8. Planning Overhead Versus Simply Retrieving
Producing a retrieval plan before searching delays the very first search, the same upfront latency cost covered generally in Planning.
It is worthwhile once that upfront cost is repaid by more accurate final retrieval.
9. Recognizing When Retrieval Planning Earns Its Upfront Cost

blocks.alt: A query needing multiple search steps points toward retrieval planning

blocks.text: Complex queries needing several different search strategies benefit from a retrieval plan.
A query answerable with one straightforward search, by contrast, does not need a retrieval plan at all.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using one uniform search strategy for a query that actually needs several different strategies.
Executing planned searches in an order that ignores real dependencies between them.
Continuing to the next planned search after an earlier search returns nothing useful.
Building a full retrieval plan for a query answerable with one straightforward search.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Retrieval planning decides the retrieval strategy for a query before executing any search.
It narrows general agentic planning specifically to sequencing retrieval calls.
It estimates the number of searches a query will actually require before running any of them.
Different parts of a complex query can call for different retrieval strategies within one plan.
A later search often depends on an earlier search's result, so search order is not arbitrary.
Retrieval planning mixes strategies within a query, a finer grain than routing the whole query.
A search returning nothing useful can invalidate the rest of the plan, requiring revision.
Producing a plan before searching adds upfront latency, worthwhile when it improves accuracy.
